# A Representation Bake-Off {#sec-bake-off}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The numbers and code outputs on this page come
from real runs on one machine, with `scikit-learn` 1.9.0, `gensim` 4.4.0,
NumPy 2.5.2 and pandas 3.0.5 on Python 3.12.13. The data is public. The code
shown is abridged to explain the main steps; reproducing every table also
needs the full data-splitting, training and reporting steps. The timings
reported belong to runs on that one machine.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- build a pipeline from raw text to an evaluated prediction for a real,
  imbalanced dataset, using the methods of the previous two chapters
  (@sec-text-as-data, @sec-embeddings);
- explain why accuracy alone is not enough on this imbalanced task, compute
  macro-F1 from its per-class arithmetic, and discuss when a different business
  goal calls for a different metric;
- form a starting expectation for count and embedding representations on a
  task by weighing the amount of labelled and unlabelled data, the structure of
  the task, the preprocessing and the tuning budget together — and then test
  that expectation with an experiment;
- measure the out-of-vocabulary rate on Turkish text, and evaluate separately
  which new word forms fastText can produce a vector for, how good those
  vectors are, and what they do to the task score;
- show with an example the word-order information that a unigram bag and an
  average of word vectors both lose, and explain which distinctions longer
  n-grams and order-sensitive models can bring back.

**What we will look at.** One dataset of Turkish reviews, with count and
embedding representations compared under one shared evaluation protocol. A
*bake-off*, in the engineering sense, is a controlled comparison of this kind:
several candidate methods, one task, one protocol, and the same measuring stick
for all of them. We first settle the metric that suits the class imbalance and
the preprocessing, then look at each method's score, coverage, cost and
errors. Finally we show how the result changes as the amount of labelled data
changes, and which word-order information both representation families are
blind to.

## Comparing two representation families on one task {#two-chapters-one-argument-to-settle}

@sec-text-as-data taught you to count words. @sec-embeddings taught you to
place them as coordinates. Each chapter ended with a claim. The two claims do
not logically contradict each other — a sparse classifier *can* be strong
while a word-level vocabulary generalises badly across morphology at the same
time — but which one dominates on a particular dataset is something you only
learn by measuring.

::: {#gloss-baseline .column-margin .term-gloss}
**baseline** — the reference result a new method is judged against, on the
same data and the same metric. A plain majority-class rule can be a baseline,
and so can a strong TF-IDF system. Reading a score also takes the class
distribution and the cost of each kind of error. [↩](#term-baseline){.term-back}
:::

::: {#gloss-agglutinative .column-margin .term-gloss}
**agglutinative** — describes a language in which morphemes mostly attach to
the word as separable affixes. In Turkish, inflectional and derivational
suffixes can give one root or stem many surface forms; how many depends on
usage and on the corpus. [↩](#term-agglutinative){.term-back}
:::

Chapter 2 showed that sparse count vectors can be a strong, cheap,
interpretable [baseline](#gloss-baseline){#term-baseline .term-ref}. Chapter 3
argued that giving every word form its own independent feature can leave a
coverage problem on the inflected forms of an
[agglutinative](#gloss-agglutinative){#term-agglutinative .term-ref} language
like Turkish. Its measurement was this: build the vocabulary on 90% of a
Turkish Wikipedia sample and test on the remaining 10%, and **7.33%** of test
tokens were never seen in training — and 28.99% of distinct word *types*.
Those rates belong to that sample and that definition of the vocabulary; they
are not constants of every Turkish corpus.

Both claims can hold at once. This chapter compares the two representation
families on one Turkish review task and one test set. All seven rows use
logistic regression; but the vectorisers do not share the same preprocessing,
vocabulary threshold, feature scale or extra training cost. So the results
compare these concrete setups of the methods, and we do not read the gap
between them as the effect of the representation family alone.

::: {.column-margin}
Chapter 3's own comparison ran on 20 Newsgroups: English, balanced, four
classes, 2,327 training documents. The Turkish product reviews here differ in
data, task and training protocol all at once. Where the conclusions differ, we
cannot say how much each factor contributes without comparisons that change
them one at a time.
:::

The setup is deliberately plain. Four things are the same in every row: the
train/test split, the `LogisticRegression` class, the class weighting and the
random seed. What changes from row to row is the vectoriser's vocabulary
threshold, the tokenisation path, the scale of the features, and the separate
training of the dense representations on unlabelled text. So a difference in
score may be decided by the representation together with these accompanying
design choices.

Holding a hyperparameter fixed is not the same as being fair to every
representation. Every row of the main comparison uses `C = 1.0`. `C` is
logistic regression's regularisation setting; in scikit-learn it is the
*inverse* of the penalty strength, so a smaller `C` shrinks the coefficients
harder. How hard a given `C` actually shrinks depends on the scale of the
features. `TfidfVectorizer` L2-normalises its rows by default, so in the TF-IDF
rows every document arrives with norm 1.0; the averaged word2vec and fastText
vectors are not normalised and their norms vary. The same `C` need not mean the
same regularisation on those two scales. In the main comparison `C` was not
searched for any row (one later ablation tunes it for two sparse rows only). A
fairer design gives each representation a comparable validation budget for its
`C` and its normalisation option; it states which data the vocabulary, the IDF
weights and the embeddings were fitted on, and it keeps the test labels out of
the selection. This version does not do that, which is a real limitation and
is flagged again where it matters.

## The problem

We set the comparison up as a binary sentiment task on Turkish product
reviews, with imbalanced classes and inconsistent spelling.

**Turkish product reviews, labelled positive or negative.** The dataset
published by Fatih Barmanbay holds 235,165 reviews and is distributed as a
single parquet file [@barmanbay2020turkishreviews]. Its card says the reviews
were collected online; it does not document which site they came from, when,
or how the labels were produced. The texts are short and informal:
misspellings, missing diacritics, run-together words. They are not raw either:
all of the distributed text has already been lowercased (measured below).

We chose this dataset for three reasons:

1. **It is Turkish**, so chapter 3's morphology argument (@sec-embeddings) can
   be tested on real user text.
2. **Its classes are imbalanced** — the positive class is 14.8 times
   larger — so the choice of evaluation metric has to be argued.
3. **It is large enough to subsample**, so we can compare how the methods
   behave as the amount of labelled training data changes. That last
   comparison is a learning curve valid for this data and these settings.

```python
import hashlib
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

URL = ("https://huggingface.co/datasets/fthbrmnby/turkish_product_reviews/"
       "resolve/main/data/train-00000-of-00001.parquet")
df = pd.read_parquet(URL).rename(
    columns={"sentence": "text", "sentiment": "label"})
print(f"missing text or label   {int(df.isna().any(axis=1).sum()):>7,}")
df["text"] = df["text"].astype(str).str.strip()
labels_per_text = df.groupby("text")["label"].nunique()
print(f"empty texts             {int(df['text'].eq('').sum()):>7,}")
print(f"texts with both labels  {int(labels_per_text.gt(1).sum()):>7,}")
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="text")
```

```text
### checks before de-duplication
missing text or label         0
empty texts                  21
texts with both labels       77
```

```text
### the raw data
rows as downloaded      235,165
after de-duplication    233,508      (1,657 exact duplicates removed)
label 1 (positive)      218,747      93.7%
label 0 (negative)       14,761       6.3%
```

The first three lines are the checks made before de-duplication. Nothing is
missing. 21 rows have an empty text; de-duplication collapses them into one
row. 77 texts carry both labels (297 rows in all): the same short review is
labelled positive in one place and negative in another. `drop_duplicates`
keeps the first row in which each text appears; in this file every positive
review comes before every negative one, so all 77 texts stayed with their
positive label. This chapter left that choice as it was; 17 of the 77 texts
fall inside the 50,000-review subsample below. On your own data, choose the
policy for conflicting labels — keep the first, drop them all, or decide by
hand — explicitly, and report it.

The class counts can be checked against the source. The dataset card reports
220,284 positive and 14,881 negative reviews. After de-duplicating on the text
the counts are 218,747 and 14,761; the differences are 1,537 and 120, and
$1{,}537 + 120 = 1{,}657$ — the number of duplicates removed. That agreement
shows the counts are consistent; it does not show which records
de-duplication kept. The check above does.

::: {.column-margin}
**Provenance, and what is not documented.** The dataset was compiled by Fatih
Barmanbay [@barmanbay2020turkishreviews]. The licence is stated differently in
two places: the licensing section of the card and the licence file of the
original GitHub repository say **CC BY-SA 4.0**, while the licence field at
the top of the Hugging Face page says "unknown" (checked on 10 October 2026).
CC BY-SA is share-alike, a stricter licence than this book's own CC BY 4.0, so
check the original repository's licence and the card together before you
redistribute the data or anything derived from it. Three things the card does
not say: which site was scraped, when, and **how the positive/negative label
was derived** — a star-rating threshold, manual annotation, something else.
That last gap matters, because @sec-data-annotation is built entirely on the
label quality of this corpus and has to work without knowing how the labels
were made.
:::

The same text sitting on both sides of the train/test split can, especially
with short reviews, let a memorised answer score as a generalisation. That is
why this experiment de-duplicates on the text *before* splitting; the 1,657
duplicates are only 0.7% of the file. The step is necessary but not sufficient
on its own: templated or near-duplicate texts can survive it, and a text that
carries two different labels needs its own decision. Report the
de-duplication policy you chose together with the dataset.

We then take a stratified 50,000-review subsample of the 233,508
de-duplicated reviews, preserving the class ratio, and split it 80/20, again
stratified:

```python
sub, _ = train_test_split(df, train_size=50_000,
                          stratify=df["label"], random_state=42)
train, test = train_test_split(sub, test_size=0.2,
                               stratify=sub["label"], random_state=42)

def fingerprint(frame):
    rows = ",".join(map(str, sorted(frame.index)))
    return hashlib.sha256(rows.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]

for name, part in [("train", train), ("test", test)]:
    pos = int(part["label"].sum())
    print(f"{name:<6} {len(part):>7,}   {pos:>7,} positive   "
          f"{len(part) - pos:>6,} negative   rows {fingerprint(part)}")
```

```text
### the split (stratified, seed 42)
train   40,000    37,471 positive    2,529 negative   rows 8205c2be5ebf
test    10,000     9,368 positive      632 negative   rows 634cdb3bb002
```

The `rows` column is a digest computed from the positions of the selected rows
in the raw file. If your own run prints the same 12 characters, you selected
the same rows. The class totals do not show that; many other splits give the
same totals.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Two warnings about this split.**

*Reproducing it.* The first version of this chapter recorded the split only as
"stratified with seed 42". That does not name a procedure; it names a *family*
of procedures, and they disagree: it does not say which call did the sampling,
in which order, or in how many stages. The two calls above were recovered
later; the story is in @sec-classification. The numbers 50,000, 40,000 and
10,000, and the **101,659 features** from the bigram vectoriser, are strong
diagnostic signs — a plausible alternative construction yields 100,350
features instead, as you will see there — but they are not proof that you
selected the same rows. The proof is a matching row digest, or the exact
sampling code. @sec-clustering, drawing from the same source with the same
seed, ended up with a *different* 50,000 rows.

*The test set and selection.* Every number below is read off the same 10,000
test reviews: seven representations, nine training sizes, a hybrid, three
diagnostics. Read these results as exploratory: you cannot pick a method or a
crossover point from these rows and then report an unbiased final score on the
same rows. In real work, split `train` again, select on that validation slice,
and use the test set only for the final evaluation. @sec-classification does
precisely that, and says why it had to.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
Subsampling to 50,000 is a convenience, not a necessity: it shortens the
experiment. Keeping the same 10,000 test reviews and training on all of the
other 223,508 reviews leaves the ranking unchanged, and every row gains
(macro-F1, single run): bag of words 73.51 → 74.50; TF-IDF 71.95 → 73.00;
bigram TF-IDF 76.21 → 76.69; character TF-IDF 70.39 → 71.12; averaged
word2vec 61.39 → 62.89; averaged fastText 61.36 → 62.84; doc2vec
55.13 → 61.99.
:::

## The class error the first score hides {#the-trap-in-the-first-number-you-will-compute}

Before comparing the methods, we use the simplest possible rule — always pick
the majority class — to show which errors accuracy can hide on an imbalanced
test set.

Predict "positive" for every review. Never look at the text at all.

```text
### the majority-class baseline
accuracy   93.68%
```

A rule that only ever predicts "positive" reaches 93.68% accuracy without
using the review text at all, because 93.68% of the test set is positive. That
score does not say whether the rule can find the negative reviews. The
confusion matrix does:

```text
### majority baseline, in full
                 predicted neg   predicted pos   total
   actual neg          0             632          632
   actual pos          0           9,368        9,368

precision (neg)   undefined — it never predicts negative
recall    (neg)   0.0%       — it finds none of the 632
F1        (neg)   0.00       — 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN) = 0 / 632
F1        (pos)   96.74
macro-F1          48.37
```

**Macro-F1 is the equally weighted average of the per-class F1 scores**: each
class gets the same weight regardless of its size. The majority rule scores
F1 = 0 on the negative class, so its macro-F1 stays at 48.37. That makes
visible what the 93.68% accuracy hides. The decision metric for a real system
still has to be chosen separately, from the costs of its errors.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why macro-F1, spelled out with the actual arithmetic

So on this dataset accuracy cannot be the decision metric on its own. What
replaces it, and why does that replacement not have
the same problem?

For one class, with $TP$ true positives, $FP$ false positives and $FN$ false
negatives:

$$
\text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}, \qquad
\text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}, \qquad
F_1 = \frac{2 \cdot \text{precision} \cdot \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}}
    = \frac{2\,TP}{2\,TP + FP + FN}
$$

$F_1$ is the *harmonic* mean of precision and recall. When either of them
drops to zero, so does $F_1$: with precision 1.00 and recall 0.00 the
arithmetic mean is 0.50 and $F_1$ is 0.00. That property keeps the misses in
one class from being hidden behind a single high precision.

Mind the zero denominators. If a class is never predicted ($TP + FP = 0$) its
precision is undefined; $F_1$ can still be computed from the second form,
which is written in counts. $F_1$ is undefined only when $TP = FP = FN = 0$,
that is, when the class has neither true nor predicted examples; in that case
scikit-learn reads what to return from its `zero_division` argument.

Macro-F1 then averages across classes:

$$
\text{macro-}F_1 = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} F_1^{(k)}
$$

For the majority baseline the negative class has $TP = 0$, $FP = 0$ and
$FN = 632$, so $F_1^{(\text{neg})} = 0/632 = 0$, and

$$
F_1^{(\text{pos})} = \frac{2 \cdot 0.9368 \cdot 1.0}{0.9368 + 1.0} = 0.9674,
$$

so macro-F1 $= (0 + 0.9674)/2 = 0.4837$.

**Which F1 your library reports.** "F1" alone is ambiguous, and in
scikit-learn the `average` argument decides it. The default for two classes,
`average="binary"`, reports the F1 of class 1 only — here the *majority*
positive class, so the majority rule scores 96.74. `average="micro"` pools all
the counts before dividing; for single-label classification with every class
included, that equals accuracy (93.68). `average="weighted"` weights each
class's F1 by its number of examples, which gives 90.62 on this class
distribution. `average="macro"`, which weights the classes equally, gives
48.37. Always write the argument out explicitly.

**Accuracy weights examples equally; macro-F1 weights classes equally.** On a
test set where only 6.32% of the reviews are negative, calling everything
"positive" gives 93.68% accuracy and catches no complaint at all. A system
that triages product reviews has to set the cost of a missed complaint and of
a false alarm separately. Macro-F1 is used here as a comparison metric that
weights the two classes equally; it is not the only possible product metric.

Every model below uses `class_weight="balanced"`. It sets the class weights
from the inverse of the class counts in the training set. With the 37,471
positive and 2,529 negative training examples here, the class coefficient of a
negative example in the loss is about 14.8 times that of a positive one. That
does not mean the gradients of individual examples carry the same ratio; a
gradient also depends on the features and on the predicted probability. This
chapter did not measure the unweighted setup; exercise 2 asks you to.

Do not conflate the two: choosing macro-F1 as the **headline metric** and
**reweighting** the training loss by class frequency are separate design
decisions. One sets what the evaluation cares about, the other what training
cares about, and picking one does not automatically bring the other. Balanced
class weights are a strong default, but compare unweighted, weighted and
threshold-tuned variants on a validation set.
:::

In this chapter **macro-F1 is the main summary score for comparing the
methods, and accuracy is reported alongside it for context.** Watch how the
two columns diverge in the tables. Macro-F1 is not a universal answer: in a
real system that processes reviews, recall on the negative class, precision
at a given false-alarm budget, or expected business cost can be more direct
decision metrics.

## Tokenising Turkish, and the trap inside that

Before the count and embedding models, we define the preprocessing decisions
both of them will use. We look at the Turkish-specific lowercasing that
chapter 2 mentioned (@sec-text-as-data) on this data, and then show which
characters the tokeniser keeps and which it throws away. The details of the
conversion are in the Turkish NLP chapter (@sec-turkish-nlp).

```python
"IYI".lower()          # → 'iyi'
"İYİ".lower()          # → 'i̇yi̇'   (an i with an extra combining dot)
```

In Turkish, dotted `i`/`İ` and dotless `ı`/`I` are different letters that
distinguish different words. Lowercasing correctly spelled Turkish text needs
the mapping `I → ı` and `İ → i`; that is one of the language-specific
tailorings the Unicode standard defines and the default does not apply.
Python's `str.lower()` implements Unicode's *default* case mapping — the
language-independent one — and does not change with the locale: it produces
`i` for `I`, and `i` plus a combining dot (U+0307) for `İ`. In text typed on
an ASCII keyboard, this mapping alone cannot tell which letter the writer
meant; we come back to that limit below.

```python
TR_LOWER = str.maketrans({"I": "ı", "İ": "i"})
def tr_lower(s):
    return s.translate(TR_LOWER).lower()

tr_lower("IYI")        # → 'ıyı'
tr_lower("İYİ")        # → 'iyi'
```

```text
### the same string, two lowercasing rules
             str.lower()      tr_lower()
"IYI"        iyi              ıyı
"İYİ"        i̇yi̇             iyi
```

The default operation cannot turn correctly spelled `IYI` and `İYİ` into
their Turkish lowercase forms: it makes `IYI` into `iyi`, and it leaves a
combining dot in `İYİ`. Both run without an error, and both can break
tokenisation and vocabulary matching. In this experiment's main score,
however, no difference was measured between the two lowercasing routines,
because the distributed data is already lowercase (shown below the round 1
table); combining-dot damage that already exists needs a separate repair
step. **Case conversion is language-dependent, and a language-specific
lowercasing policy is part of the preprocessing and tokeniser contract.** (The operation here is lowercasing; Unicode *casefolding* is a
related but distinct operation intended for caseless matching, and it has its
own Turkish tailoring.) One limit up front: `tr_lower` assumes correct
spelling. In user text typed on an English keyboard, `IYI` may well mean "İYİ",
and `tr_lower` then produces `ıyı`, a new error. What ASCII-typed text needs
is the restoration of Turkish characters (deasciification; see
@sec-turkish-nlp-normalization).

::: {.column-margin}
Case mappings that depend on the locale or on the context matter in other
languages too: in Greek, a sigma at the end of a word lowercases to `ς`, not
`σ`. German `ß` belongs to a different operation: `"ß".lower()` leaves it
unchanged, and it is casefolding that equates `ß` with `ss`
(`"ß".casefold()` → `ss`). That is why the "just lowercase it" step in an
English tutorial is not portable advice; but do not treat these examples as
the same problem as Turkish `I`/`İ` either.
:::

After Turkish lowercasing, the simple token pattern we use extracts unbroken
runs of a chosen set of lowercase letters:

```python
import re
TOKEN_RE = re.compile(r"[a-zçğıöşü]+")
def tokenize(s):
    return TOKEN_RE.findall(tr_lower(s))
```

The pattern keeps only the listed letters: punctuation, digits and emoji all
disappear, and circumflexed letters (`â`, `î`, `û`) and combining marks split
a token. `hâlâ` or `kâr`, for example, does not survive as one token. In
product reviews `!!!`, `5/5` or an emoji can carry sentiment; this experiment
does not model them. The effect of these simplifications on the classification
score was not measured; on your own corpus, compare alternative patterns.

With this tokeniser the training corpus looks like this:

```text
### the training corpus, 40,000 reviews
tokens                        903,190
distinct word forms            74,317
hapax (seen exactly once)      43,579     58.6% of all forms
mean review length               22.6 tokens
median                             19
95th percentile                    56
longest                           296
```

::: {.column-margin}
Of the 74,317 distinct forms, 43,579 occur exactly once; the other 30,738 are
seen at least twice. After `min_df=2` the vectoriser has 30,195 columns. We
counted the **543** forms in between one by one: every one of them occurs two
or more times in the corpus but only inside *one document*. `min_df` counts
**document** frequency, not corpus frequency.
:::

**58.6% of the vocabulary appears exactly once.** In chapter 3's Turkish
Wikipedia sample the rate was 50.0% (@sec-embeddings). The two corpora differ
in topic, document length and preprocessing, so the gap cannot be put down to
typos alone; the spelling variation of user-generated text is one possible
factor.

The variety of forms becomes visible if you group word forms by their first
five characters:

```text
### distinct word forms sharing a five-character prefix
kulla    895 forms   kullanışlı, kullanıyorum, kullandım, kullanımı, kullanım, ...
bekle    285 forms   beklediğimden, beklediğim, beklemiyordum, beklemeyin, ...
çalış    247 forms   çalışıyor, çalışma, çalışan, çalışması, çalışırken, ...
çıkar    209 forms   çıkarıyor, çıkar, çıkartıyor, çıkarmıyor, çıkardı, ...
düşün    195 forms   düşünüyorum, düşünmeden, düşünenlere, düşünen, ...
```

::: {#gloss-bag-of-words .column-margin .term-gloss}
**bag-of-words** — count which words a document contains and forget the
order they came in. "Dog bites man" and "man bites dog" become the same
document. [↩](#term-bag-of-words){.term-back}
:::

The five-character prefix `kulla` appears in 895 distinct forms in this
corpus. The group is not 895 inflections of one stem: it holds inflections,
derivations and spelling variants together. In a
[bag-of-words](#gloss-bag-of-words){#term-bag-of-words .term-ref} model every
form that enters the training vocabulary becomes its own column (with
`min_df=2` the forms seen in only one review never become columns at all —
they are simply dropped). The coefficient learned for `kullanışlı` does not
transfer by itself to the `kullanıyorum` column; other features in the same
document, and regularisation, still affect how the model generalises.

A five-character prefix is a crude look at the variety of Turkish word forms;
it is not stem or morpheme analysis. The `kulla` group puts `kullanışlı` (an
adjective), `kullanım` (a noun) and `kullanıcı` (a noun) side by side, and the
same prefix also collects typos. So this table does not measure how many
columns a real stem family is spread over. Finding that out takes
morphological analysis and a separate look at the spelling variants; the
analysis is classically done with finite-state transducers [@oflazer1994two].
For Turkish morphological analysers and how to use them, see
@sec-turkish-nlp-analysis and @sec-turkish-resources-tools.

The 895-form prefix group is a sign of how far the number of word-level
features can grow. Below we look separately at how this variety relates to
coverage and to the classification score.

## Round 1 — the chapter-2 methods

We have chosen the evaluation metric and defined Turkish lowercasing
explicitly. The combining-dot errors already present in the data are still
there; we come back to them below the table. Now we compare the four count
representations of chapter 2 (@sec-text-as-data) with the same classifier.

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer, TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

PAT = r"[a-zçğıöşü]+"
# lowercase=False + preprocessor=tr_lower: otherwise scikit-learn calls
# Python's str.lower() and commits the bug we warned about above
LOC = dict(preprocessor=tr_lower, lowercase=False)
schemes = {
  "bag of words":    CountVectorizer(min_df=2, token_pattern=PAT, **LOC),
  "tf-idf":          TfidfVectorizer(min_df=2, sublinear_tf=True, token_pattern=PAT, **LOC),
  "tf-idf 1-2 gram": TfidfVectorizer(min_df=2, sublinear_tf=True,
                                     ngram_range=(1, 2), token_pattern=PAT, **LOC),
    # a separate feature-extraction path: token_pattern is not used, and min_df differs
  "tf-idf char_wb 3-5": TfidfVectorizer(min_df=3, sublinear_tf=True,
                                        analyzer="char_wb", ngram_range=(3, 5), **LOC),
}
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=42)
```

```text
### round 1: counting
                      accuracy   macro-F1   F1(neg)   dims      fit
majority baseline        93.68      48.37      0.00      —        —
bag of words             92.14      73.51     51.30   30,195    0.7 s
tf-idf                   90.07      71.95     49.41   30,195    0.5 s
tf-idf 1-2 gram          92.57      76.21     56.47  101,659    1.0 s
tf-idf char_wb 3-5       88.63      70.39     47.14   94,939    3.3 s
```

The rows of the table share the same train/test split and the same
classifier; but they differ from one another in three respects.

**The character row does not go through the same tokeniser.** In
`scikit-learn`, `token_pattern` is used only when `analyzer="word"`; `char_wb`
ignores it entirely and runs its own character stream. So the character row
differs from the word rows not only in feature granularity but in the
feature-extraction path itself:

```text
### the same string through the two analyzers
input:  "5/5 harika!! ürün çok i̇yi 👍"

analyzer="word", token_pattern=[a-zçğıöşü]+
  ['harika', 'ürün', 'çok', 'i', 'yi']
  — 5/5, !!, the emoji are gone; the combining dot split "i̇yi" in two

analyzer="char_wb", ngram_range=(3, 5)     (first few of the 3-grams)
  [' 5/', '5/5', '/5 ', ' ha', 'har', 'ari', 'rik', 'ika', 'ka!', 'a!!', '!! ', ...]
  — digits, the slash, the exclamation marks and the spaces all survive as features
```

So the score difference of the character row may reflect this preprocessing
choice along with the character features: `char_wb` does not apply the word
token pattern, and it treats digits, punctuation and spaces differently. Keep
that in mind when you read the conclusions this chapter draws from character
n-grams later on.

The character scheme uses `min_df=3` where the three word schemes use
`min_df=2`. That is a defensible choice — character n-gram counts explode — but
it is a choice, it was not swept, and this chapter did not measure what the
other setting would have done.

The `fit` column here and the `build the representation` column in the cost
table near the end of the chapter do not time the same step. Re-measured five
times each, vectorising the training text took 0.82–0.90 s for the bigram
scheme and 2.68–2.79 s for the character scheme; fitting the classifier took
0.09–0.10 s and 0.38–0.39 s respectively. The gaps between the two tables
(1.0 s against 0.9 s; 3.3 s against 2.9 s) are consistent with the classifier's
fitting time: `fit` covers vectorising plus fitting the classifier, the cost
table covers vectorising only. The timings in the tables come from single
runs, and the hybrid's cost arithmetic later uses the second set; read all of
them as approximate values for this machine.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## It made no difference on this corpus — write it this way anyway

The `lowercase=False` line above was added later, because the first version
committed exactly the bug this chapter warns about two sections earlier. Both
versions were then measured, and round 1's table came out **byte-identical**.

The reason is the corpus itself: there is **not a single uppercase character**
among the 37,076,865 characters of the 233,508 de-duplicated reviews (counted
with `str.isupper()`). That observation is consistent with the distributed
text having been lowercased beforehand; the dataset card does not document
with which tool, or when. So the two paths coincide here.

That is not the same as the corpus being clean. U+0307 (COMBINING DOT ABOVE)
sits in **4,194 documents of the 50,000-review working subsample — 8.4% of
it**, and every time it follows a letter `i`. Unicode's default lowercasing
produces exactly that sequence for `İ`. The earlier processing steps of the
data are not documented, so we cannot settle where the mark came from; the
observation is consistent with such a conversion. Our own `[a-zçğıöşü]+`
pattern does not treat a combining mark as a word character, so in those
documents `tavsiye` splits into `tavsi` + `ye`. We measured the effect on the
vocabulary: deleting the mark and re-vectorising the training text takes the
30,195-column vocabulary down to 29,823. **595 columns exist only because of
this splitting** (`alişveri`, `alabi` and the like); after the repair, 223
forms that had never appeared in one piece enter the vocabulary.
@sec-clustering rediscovers the same damage in its own sample as a clustering
result and measures it line by line. `tr_lower` does not delete a combining
dot that is already in the text — the repair is to delete the mark from the
text you were given, not to lowercase it differently. Exercise 7 asks you to
measure what the repair does to the scores.

Why fix it anyway? Because the reader copying this code will not have that
corpus. A small illustration of the difference:

```text
'İYİ'.lower()  ->  'i̇yi̇'  ->  under [a-zçğıöşü]+  ['i', 'yi']   split in two
'IYI'.lower()  ->  'iyi'   ->                      ['iyi']       wrongly merged
```

The same warning applies to `analyzer="char_wb"`. Character n-grams are sold
as language-independent, but the lowercasing step in front of them is still
locale-dependent.
:::

Three things in that table are worth stopping for.

::: {#gloss-f1-score-macro-f1 .column-margin .term-gloss}
**F1 score / macro-F1** — F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall
for one class. Macro-F1 averages the F1 of every class with equal weight, so a
rare class counts as much as a common one. In this experiment it is the metric
that makes the majority rule's F1 = 0 on the negative class visible. [↩](#term-f1-score-macro-f1){.term-back}
:::

**Accuracy and [macro-F1](#gloss-f1-score-macro-f1){#term-f1-score-macro-f1 .term-ref} part ways over the majority rule.** All four
count methods have lower accuracy than the majority rule's 93.68%, while
scoring 22 to 28 macro-F1 points above it. (Among the four methods the two
metrics give the same order: bag-of-words, for example, has both higher
accuracy and higher macro-F1 than TF-IDF.) The models evaluated here give up
some of the accuracy that ignoring the minority provides, and gain
negative-class recall in return. If you chose a method by accuracy alone in
this setup, the majority rule would look like a strong candidate. That is not
a law: other thresholds and training settings can raise both accuracy and
performance on the negative class; we did not test those options here.

**In this setup raw counts are ahead of TF-IDF.** The first explanation that
comes to mind is IDF: reviews average 22.6 tokens, most words appear once in a
document, so IDF may be down-weighting the frequent sentiment words — `güzel`,
`iyi`, `tavsiye`. That is a hypothesis, and a testable one, because **three**
things change at once between `CountVectorizer` and `TfidfVectorizer`: IDF
weighting, sublinear term
frequency (`sublinear_tf=True`, which replaces a count $c$ by $1 + \log c$),
and the L2 row normalisation
`TfidfVectorizer` applies by default. Turn each on and off separately — same
vocabulary, same classifier, same `C = 1.0`:

```text
### one change at a time, unigram word features, min_df=2
                                    idf   log-TF   norm   accuracy  macro-F1  F1(neg)
raw counts  (= "bag of words")       no     no     none     92.14     73.51    51.30
counts + L2                          no     no      L2      88.07     69.57    45.85
log-TF + L2                          no     yes     L2      88.37     70.00    46.53
counts + idf + L2                    yes    no      L2      90.20     72.16    49.74
log-TF + idf, no norm                yes    yes    none     92.67     71.83    47.61
log-TF + idf + L2  (= "tf-idf")      yes    yes     L2      90.07     71.95    49.41
```

The result does not support the first explanation. With `C = 1.0` fixed,
adding **L2 row normalisation** to raw counts takes macro-F1 from 73.51 down
to 69.57 (3.94 points); IDF, *added on top of it*, brings the score up to
72.16. So the original gap does not come from IDF alone, and "TF-IDF fell
behind here because of IDF" is not what the experiment shows. Nor does it mean
normalisation is harmful in itself: its effect has to be judged together with
`C`.

A likely explanation is that we did not tune `C`. L2-normalised rows have norm
1 while raw count rows grow with document length, so a fixed `C = 1.0` applies
a different effective regularisation to the two representations — the same
caveat this chapter flagged up front for the dense family, now inside the
sparse one. Give both the same small tuning budget: split the 40,000 training
documents into 32,000 for fitting and 8,000 for validation, choose `C` on the
validation slice, then refit with the chosen `C` on all 40,000 documents and
measure on the test set:

```text
### C chosen on a validation split carved out of train (32,000 fit / 8,000 val)
                     best C on validation    test macro-F1
raw counts                  1.0                  73.51
tf-idf                     10.0                  74.71
```

The selection step is spelled out because it changes the result: the test
scores in the table belong to models refitted with the chosen `C` on all
40,000 documents (the 32,000-document models score 73.65 and 73.83 on the same
test set). This test set was already used earlier in the chapter, so these
rows are not an independent test result opened for the first time.

The ordering flips: with `C` chosen on validation, TF-IDF scores 74.71
macro-F1 and raw counts 73.51. We measured how solid that 1.2-point gap is on
this test set by pairing the two models' predictions on the same 10,000 test
reviews. Over 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples the 95% interval of the
macro-F1 difference runs from 0.42 to 1.99 points; there are 151 reviews only
TF-IDF gets right and 80 only raw counts get right (exact McNemar test on the
error rates, $p < 0.001$; round 2 explains how the two tests differ). So the
gap is larger than the sampling noise of this test set. The interval belongs
to one training split and one test set; it does not say what would happen on
another training sample. What the experiment shows is this: **the "raw counts
ahead of TF-IDF" result in the round 1 table did not survive an equal tuning
budget; it is not a fixed property of the representations, it depended on a
shared, untuned `C`.** The table is not wrong — that is genuinely what was
measured — but the lesson to take from it is not "TF-IDF falls behind on short
text": it is that *a representation comparison run without an equal tuning
budget may not be measuring what you wanted it to measure.*

::: {#gloss-bigram .column-margin .term-gloss}
**bigram** — a pair of words counted as a single unit, so that *not good*
can be told apart from *good*. [↩](#term-bigram){.term-back}
:::

**In this setup word unigram + [bigram](#gloss-bigram){#term-bigram .term-ref} TF-IDF scores 4.26 macro-F1 points above
unigram-only TF-IDF, and 2.70 above raw counts.** (Not the largest gaps in the
chapter — the two families are 14.8 points apart, and embeddings lead counts
by 14.6 points at 250 labels. This is the largest difference measured within
the count family once the label budget is fixed.) Bigrams keep local
sequences such as `iyi değil` ("not good") and `güzel değil` ("not nice") as
separate features, which can help capture negation built with a separate
word. The same bigrams also pick up multi-word sentiment phrases, product
names and collocations. Part of Turkish negation, though, is a suffix:
`beğendim` ("I liked it") and `beğenmedim` ("I did not like it") are separate
features at the unigram level too. In pairs like `tavsiye etmem` ("I do not
recommend") or `memnun kalmadım` ("I was not satisfied") the negation is again
a suffix: `etmem` and `kalmadım` are strong negative unigrams in the table
below, and the bigram adds the `tavsiye` or `memnun` context to them. This
chapter did not measure how much of the 4.26 points comes from which kind of
negation; saying that takes a targeted error analysis or an ablation.

### What the model learned, in words

In this sparse linear model every vocabulary feature has one coefficient.
Sorting the coefficients together with their feature names helps you inspect
which features the model has associated with each class on this data and with
this preprocessing; it does not give the effect of a word in every context.

```text
### tf-idf + logistic regression, largest coefficients
towards POSITIVE                     towards NEGATIVE
gayet        +8.04  (quite)          etmiyorum    -8.16  (I do not [recommend])
ederim       +6.94  ([I] do)         değil        -6.95  (not)
mükemmel     +6.13  (perfect)        kötü         -6.63  (bad)
teşekkürler  +6.09  (thanks)         etmem        -6.35  (I would not)
harika       +5.93  (wonderful)      beğenmedim   -6.21  (I did not like it)
memnunum     +5.84  (I am pleased)   iade         -5.85  (return / refund)
güzel        +5.48  (nice)           fakat        -5.52  (however)
süper        +4.98  (super)          kalitesiz    -5.47  (low quality)
kaliteli     +4.32  (good quality)   kalmadım     -5.33  (I was not [satisfied])
```

Two features in the list look as if they are about the domain rather than
about language: `iade` ("refund") and `fakat` ("however") are among the
features this model associates with the negative class. `iade` may refer to a
return that happened; it may also only mention the possibility of one. `fakat`
may be joining a positive judgement to a negative one. The coefficients show a
conditional association with the training labels; which reading holds has to
be checked by reading example reviews. Nobody wrote these associations down by
hand; they were learned from 40,000 labelled reviews.

Do not read the list as more than it is. The coefficients are not universal
sentiment scores for the words; they are global associations learned on *this*
training distribution, together with every other feature. On a single
document, the contribution of feature $j$ to the linear decision score is
$x_j \beta_j$; the intercept and the contributions of the other features are
added to the total score, and the probability is computed by applying the
sigmoid to that total. The global coefficient list tells you what the model
learned; it is not a complete explanation of one particular prediction. Those
are separate questions.

Keep this column in mind when the dense methods arrive, because they do not
give you the same direct word-to-coefficient table for free.

## Round 2 — the chapter-3 methods

Now the same task with the three models of chapter 3 (@sec-embeddings).
The word2vec, fastText and doc2vec models were trained from scratch on the
text of the 40,000 training reviews, without using the labels; no pretrained
vectors and no test reviews went into that training. Later, in the learning
curve, the classifier sees fewer labels while this fixed representation,
learned from the text of all 40,000 reviews, stays in use.

```python
from gensim.models import Word2Vec, FastText
from gensim.models.doc2vec import Doc2Vec, TaggedDocument

w2v = Word2Vec(train_tok, vector_size=100, window=5, min_count=2,
               sg=1, negative=5, epochs=10, workers=1, seed=42)
ft  = FastText(train_tok, vector_size=100, window=5, min_count=2,
               sg=1, negative=5, epochs=10, workers=1, seed=42,
               min_n=3, max_n=6, bucket=500_000)
d2v = Doc2Vec([TaggedDocument(d, [i]) for i, d in enumerate(train_tok)],
              vector_size=100, min_count=2, epochs=20, dm=0,
              negative=5, workers=1, seed=42)
```

The code above shows only the training settings of the three models; the
steps from there to a document matrix are these. For word2vec, a document's
vector is the mean of the vectors of its tokens that are in the vocabulary; a
document with no token in the vocabulary gets the zero vector. For fastText
every token of the document goes into the mean, because the model builds a
vector for out-of-vocabulary forms too, from subword vectors. doc2vec learns
the vectors of the training documents directly; the vectors of the test
documents are inferred with `infer_vector` at its default settings. All three
matrices go to the same logistic regression as in round 1.

```text
### round 2: coordinates
                      accuracy   macro-F1   F1(neg)   dims   embed train
averaged word2vec        79.92      61.39     34.64     100     14.7 s
averaged fastText        79.64      61.36     34.79     100     31.6 s
doc2vec (PV-DBOW)        71.96      55.13     27.66     100      8.5 s
```

Unlike the sparse rows, these rows cannot be reproduced to the last digit.
Re-running the same code with the same seed (42) while this chapter was being
revised gave 61.37 macro-F1 for word2vec, 61.29 for fastText and 55.44 for
doc2vec. Changing only the embedding seed (five seeds) kept word2vec between
61.57 and 62.06, and fastText between 60.86 and 61.68. Read the decimal
differences in the dense rows together with that spread.

Set against round 1:

```text
### both rounds, sorted by macro-F1
tf-idf 1-2 gram          92.57      76.21     56.47  101,659
bag of words             92.14      73.51     51.30   30,195
tf-idf                   90.07      71.95     49.41   30,195
tf-idf char_wb 3-5       88.63      70.39     47.14   94,939
averaged word2vec        79.92      61.39     34.64      100
averaged fastText        79.64      61.36     34.79      100
doc2vec (PV-DBOW)        71.96      55.13     27.66      100
majority baseline        93.68      48.37      0.00        —
```

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Do not read that ordering as a general ranking.** The row names are short;
in full, the three dense rows are averaged static vectors trained *from
scratch* on this corpus's 0.9 million tokens, not pretrained ones. The scale
of the dense vectors was not equalised and `C` was tuned for no row at all —
recall what the `C` experiment in the previous section did on the sparse side.

Every row comes from one split and one run. To measure the sampling
uncertainty of the test set, we paired the two models' predictions on the same
10,000 reviews and resampled the test rows 10,000 times (a paired bootstrap;
*both* models' macro-F1 is recomputed on each resample):

```text
### paired bootstrap on the 10,000 test reviews: macro-F1 difference, 95% interval
tf-idf 1-2 gram     - bag of words         +2.69   [ +1.60,  +3.82]
bag of words        - tf-idf               +1.56   [ +0.53,  +2.55]
tf-idf              - tf-idf char_wb 3-5   +1.57   [ +0.59,  +2.54]
tf-idf char_wb 3-5  - averaged word2vec    +9.01   [ +7.97, +10.01]
averaged word2vec   - averaged fastText    +0.08   [ -0.60,  +0.77]
averaged fastText   - doc2vec (PV-DBOW)    +5.85   [ +5.02,  +6.69]
tf-idf 1-2 gram     - averaged word2vec   +14.83   [+13.65, +16.01]
```

The dense rows are taken from the re-run mentioned above. The gap between the
families, and the adjacent gaps inside the sparse family, are larger than the
sampling noise of this test set; the gap between word2vec and fastText is not.
These intervals cover test sampling only: they do not say what happens when
the training split changes, and for the dense rows the spread over training
seeds comes on top. The wobble of the learning curve between 250 and 40,000
labels is not an uncertainty interval of this kind; those points differ both
in training size and in which documents were sampled.

Error rates need a separate test. McNemar's test compares the two methods'
*error rates*, so it is about the accuracy column, not the macro-F1 one the
ranking is sorted on. Later in the chapter, McNemar's test on the right/wrong
outcomes of plain word TF-IDF and averaged fastText on the same test documents
gives $\chi^2 = 684.2$; that supports the difference in error rate between
those two setups. A macro-F1 difference is not a paired count of errors; it
needs a paired bootstrap, as above, or a randomisation test.
@dror2018hitchhikers lays the protocol out in detail, and exercise 8 asks you
to reproduce these intervals in your own run and extend them over the training
split.
:::

::: {#gloss-recall .column-margin .term-gloss}
**recall** — of the reviews that really were negative, the share the model
found. Low recall goes with a lot of misses. [↩](#term-recall){.term-back}
:::

::: {#gloss-precision .column-margin .term-gloss}
**precision** — of the reviews the model called negative, the share that
really were. Low precision goes with a lot of false alarms. [↩](#term-precision){.term-back}
:::

**In this setup the best sparse representation is well ahead of the
from-scratch averaged embedding setup.** The gap between the best sparse
method and the best dense one is 14.8 macro-F1 points; on the negative class
it is **21.83** points of F1 — and the shape of that gap matters. (A
coincidence to disarm before it confuses you: a precision of 21.8% turns up a
few lines below. The two numbers are unrelated — this one is a difference in
F1 points, that one is a precision.) Averaged word2vec actually *finds* more
negatives (84.2% [recall](#gloss-recall){#term-recall .term-ref} against
bigram TF-IDF's 76.3%); but only 21.8% of the reviews it flags as negative
really are negative ([precision](#gloss-precision){#term-precision .term-ref}),
where the figure for bigram TF-IDF is 44.8%. These are aggregate rates over
the test set; do not read them as the probability that one new prediction is
right.

On chapter 3's 20 Newsgroups task (@sec-embeddings) the sparse method in the
comparison was also ahead of the averaged static embedding. Seeing a similar
ordering on two different datasets is a useful observation; but the language,
the class structure, the amount of training data and the preprocessing all
differ, so no general rule about document classification follows from these
two results. The rest of the chapter looks at how the ordering is affected, in
this Turkish review setup, when the number of labels and the kinds of error
change.

State the limit plainly too. All three round-2 models were trained from
scratch on the 903,190 tokens of the training reviews of *this corpus only*;
work such as @bojanowski2017enriching uses corpora at Wikipedia scale. So the
measurement above is precisely **"static embeddings trained from scratch on
0.9M tokens fell behind, in this setup, counts extracted from the same 40,000
documents"** — not "static embeddings fall behind counts". Vectors pretrained
on large Turkish corpora may give a different result; this chapter did not
measure the direction or the size of the difference. Exercise 13 is where you
measure it yourself.

What does *not* depend on corpus size is the averaging defect. No amount of
training data makes `kalite iyi fiyat kötü` and `kalite kötü fiyat iyi` stop
having cosine 1.0000, because that failure is in the pooling step, not in the
vectors. That is the transferable result of this chapter; the ranking above is
the local one.

Where the dense methods clearly differ is the *number of dimensions*: 61.39
macro-F1 from **100 numbers per document**, against 76.21 from 101,659
columns.

Do not read the number of dimensions as memory. In this experiment the dense
document matrix has 100 columns and the word TF-IDF matrix 30,195; even so,
the measured memory of the training matrices is 16.0 MB and 9.7 MB
respectively. A sparse matrix stores only the non-zero values and their
indices: a row with 19.8 non-zeros on average holds 19.8 values, not 30,195.
Fewer coordinates can be an advantage in some dense-vector structures — a
nearest-neighbour index, approximate-nearest-neighbour (ANN) search, the first
layer of a network; the actual memory and latency of search have to be
measured with the chosen index, the number of documents and the sparsity.

The ratio depends on which sparse model you compare against. A 100-dimensional
dense document vector has about 1,017 times fewer coordinates than bigram
TF-IDF's 101,659 columns, and about 302 times fewer than plain word TF-IDF's
30,195 (302 is the figure in the summary table later in this chapter). These
ratios are not, by themselves, ratios of memory, latency or product
architecture. In your target use, measure the costs of sparse retrieval, dense
retrieval and classification separately.

::: {.column-margin}
Note the direction of the dense models' errors: in this run averaged word2vec
finds 84.2% of the negative reviews — more than any sparse model — but the
precision of its negative predictions is 21.8%. That pattern of false alarms
may have as much to do with `class_weight="balanced"`, the decision threshold
and the choice of `C` as with how well the representation separates the
classes. Telling the causes apart takes threshold and class-weight ablations.
:::

## The out-of-vocabulary test

Chapter 3 made a specific promise about Turkish, one that could be proved
wrong: word2vec breaks
on unseen word forms, fastText does not. Here is the measurement on the test
set.

```text
### coverage of the 10,000 test reviews
test tokens                     229,055
outside the word2vec vocabulary  16,660     7.27% of tokens
distinct test word forms         32,573
outside the vocabulary           15,098     46.4% of forms
test reviews with no usable token     7
```

Chapter 3 measured 7.33% of tokens unseen on Turkish Wikipedia; reviews give
7.27%. The two are close, but they are not the same measurement:
@sec-embeddings built its vocabulary from every type in its 90% training
portion, while this word2vec drops every hapax (`min_count=2`), and
encyclopedia prose is not user-generated review text. Treat the agreement as a
coincidence worth noticing rather than a confirmed prediction.

The *type*-level numbers do not agree at all, and they are the ones that hurt.
Chapter 3 saw 28.99% of types unseen; here **46.4% of the distinct word forms
in the test set are not in the learned word2vec vocabulary**. Part of that gap
is the definition, not the data: "never seen in training" and "not in the
learned vocabulary" are different things, and the second also covers the
words seen once and then cut by `min_count=2`. Either way, nearly half the
distinct forms in *this* test set are, to word2vec, a `KeyError`; the rate
will of course vary from batch to batch and domain to domain.

fastText's coverage of that same set is 100%, by construction — it sums
character n-gram vectors, so any string of characters gets a vector. Here is
what those vectors are like for word forms that are genuinely absent from
training:

```text
### nearest neighbours for unseen word forms
kargolanmamış  ("not having been shipped")
  word2vec   KeyError
  fastText   kargolanmış, kargolandı, kargolanma, kargolanıp, kargolu

tavsiyelerim  ("my recommendations")
  word2vec   KeyError
  fastText   tavsiyeleri, tavsiyeler, tavsiyeederim, tavsiyedir

hızlıcana  (colloquial "nice and fast")
  word2vec   KeyError
  fastText   hızlıca, hızlıda, hızlısı, hızlıydı, hızlı
```

On coverage that is a clean win, exactly as advertised
[@bojanowski2017enriching]: every unseen form lands next to its own stem
family. But note that the first neighbour of `kargolanmamış` ("not yet
shipped") is `kargolanmış` ("shipped"), which has lost the negative suffix —
the first sign of the flaw shown below.

Now the finding that makes this chapter worth writing. Compare the two models
on words that are *in* both vocabularies:

```text
### nearest neighbours for a common word
kargo  ("shipping")
  word2vec   teslimat, gönderim, gönderi, kargoda, kargoyla, kargolama
             (delivery, dispatch, shipment — different words, same topic)
  fastText   kargocu, kargolu, kargosu, kargonuz, kargom, kargomun
             (courier, with-shipping, its-shipping, your-shipping, my-shipping)

kalitesiz  ("low quality")
  word2vec   dandik, kullanışsız, dayanıksız, uyduruk, kırılacak
             (shoddy, unusable, flimsy, fake, about-to-break)
  fastText   kalitesizmiş, kalitesizliği, kalitel, kalitesi, kalitesindeki
             (…all forms of the same stem, including "kalitesi" = quality)
```

**On these two words, word2vec's neighbours are semantic and fastText's are
orthographic.** Two words are an illustration and not a measurement, and the
honest version of this claim says so; the systematic version is a five-line
job — sample a few hundred in-vocabulary words, and report what share of each
model's top-5 neighbours share a long prefix with the query. This chapter did
not run it. Asked
what is like `kalitesiz` ("low quality"), word2vec answers with five other
ways to say a product is bad. fastText answers with the word `kalitesi`
("its quality") — which is not a synonym: it is a neutral noun form that has
lost the negative polarity `-siz` carried, and it earns its place by sharing eight leading characters.

This is @sec-embeddings' stated weakness — *assumes spelling similarity
implies meaning similarity* — becoming visible. The plausible explanation is
that the subword budget which buys perfect coverage is spent on modelling
morphology, and is taken from the budget that was modelling meaning. Read that
as a hypothesis: a two-word example cannot establish it, and the systematic
version is the prefix test described in the previous paragraph, which this
chapter did not run.

If that hypothesis is right, it also explains why, having solved the
out-of-vocabulary problem completely, fastText scores **61.36** where word2vec
scores **61.39**. Coverage went to
100%; macro-F1 was effectively unchanged in this run — a gap of 0.03 points,
well inside the noise this chapter measures on itself.

::: {.fig-cap}
The out-of-vocabulary problem is real, fastText solves it completely, and on
this task solving it changes nothing. Coverage is a property of the
representation; accuracy is a property of the representation *and the task*.
An [intrinsic](#gloss-intrinsic-extrinsic-evaluation){#term-intrinsic-extrinsic-evaluation .term-ref} fix only pays if the thing it fixed was what the task was
limited by — here, it was not.
:::
::::

::: {#gloss-intrinsic-extrinsic-evaluation .column-margin .term-gloss}
**intrinsic / extrinsic evaluation** — *intrinsic* scores the
representation on its own terms, such as how many words it covers.
*Extrinsic* scores it on the job you actually need doing. This chapter is
a long argument that only the second one settles anything. [↩](#term-intrinsic-extrinsic-evaluation){.term-back}
:::

One more diagnostic, because it corrects a natural misreading. Being *in*
the vocabulary is not the same as being *well estimated*:

```text
### kalitesizmiş — in the word2vec vocabulary, seen a handful of times
  word2vec   ayakkabıların, kaymak, yapışır, temizlenmemiş, zorlamadım
             (of the shoes, cream, it sticks, uncleaned, I did not force)
  fastText   kalitesiz, kalitesizliği, kalitesinide, kalitesi
```

word2vec has a vector for this word and the vector is noise. The 46.4%
out-of-vocabulary rate is therefore an *understatement* of the problem: past
the vocabulary boundary you get an error, which is at least honest, but just
inside it you get confident nonsense.

## Why the dense methods lost

The table says counting won. It does not say *why*, and "dense embeddings are
worse" is not an explanation — it is a restatement. So let us look at the
documents the two methods disagree about.

Take two representations: plain word TF-IDF (the 90.07-accuracy row) and
averaged fastText (79.64). They agree on 84.1% of the test set. Where they
disagree, TF-IDF is right 1,315 times and averaged fastText is right 272 —
nearly five to one. (With two classes, whenever the two disagree exactly one
of them is right, so 1,315 − 272 = 1,043 documents is exactly their accuracy
gap: 10.43 points.)

Those two counts are also the whole of a significance test, so we may as well
run it. The intuition: if the two methods were equally accurate, their
disagreements would split roughly half and half, and McNemar's test on paired
predictions [@mcnemar1947note] asks how far from half-and-half the split is.
It uses exactly these off-diagonal counts:
$\chi^2 = (|1315 - 272| - 1)^2 / (1315 + 272) = 684.2$ on one degree of
freedom, far past any conventional threshold. Read it for what it is: a test
that the two methods make errors at different rates, which is a statement
about accuracy. The macro-F1 gap is in the same direction and far larger than
the variability this chapter measures below, but confirming *it* would take a
paired bootstrap over the test rows, not this test. The sparse–dense gap is
real and nothing about it is marginal.

That is worth stating precisely *because* most of the other gaps in this
chapter are not tested at all — see the warning under the combined
leaderboard above. The interesting question is what the 272 look like.

```text
### averaged fastText right, tf-idf wrong        (gold: positive)
  "en guvenli alısveriş sitesi"        diacritics partly dropped
  "çok hizli ve temi̇z tesli̇mat"        broken diacritics mid-word
  "çok sessiz çalışıyor makina ."      "makina" — colloquial for "makine"

### tf-idf right, averaged fastText wrong
  "sıkıcı edebi yonu cok zayif"        gold negative — fastText says positive
  "koku ne çok kötü ne çok iyi"        gold negative — "neither… nor…"
  "cok guzel! kedi bayildi buna"       gold positive — fastText says negative
```

These are examples, not a systematic categorisation: classifying all 272
would make the claims much stronger, and this chapter did not do it. The dense
wins are exactly the promised ones: misspellings and missing
diacritics, where a count vector sees an unknown column and a subword model
sees a familiar shape. One of the dense losses is the promised kind too — the
second example is a `ne … ne …` construction ("neither very bad nor very
good") in which the individual words give mixed signals and the *structure*
carries the decision. But the picture is not that clean: the other two losses
are also texts with missing diacritics, so missing diacritics alone do not
hand fastText the win. These six examples illustrate both kinds; they do not
show which side wins and why.

That points at a representational failure consistent with the classification gap, and it is testable directly.

```text
### cosine between a review and its negation
                                                  averaged     tf-idf
                                                   fastText
ürünü çok beğendim / ürünü hiç beğenmedim            0.776       0.193
kesinlikle tavsiye ederim / … tavsiye etmem          0.919       0.474
kargo çok hızlı geldi / kargo çok yavaş geldi        0.943       0.572
fiyatına göre gayet kaliteli / … hiç kaliteli değil  0.892       0.690
bu üründen memnun kaldım / … memnun kalmadım         0.962       0.582
```

Averaging places a sentence and its opposite at cosine 0.78–0.96. TF-IDF
places the same pairs at 0.19–0.69. The mean of a handful of vectors is
dominated by the words the two sentences share, and in a negated pair that is
almost all of them — the one word carrying the reversal is averaged into
nothing along with everything else.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The arithmetic of why averaging dilutes negation

That explanation was qualitative. It is worth doing properly, because the
result is a formula. It does not hand you a fixed length threshold — that
depends on the norms and directions of the vectors — but it does show how the
dilution scales as the shared content grows.

Take a five-word review and its negation, differing in exactly one word:

$$
\mathbf{d}_+ = \frac{1}{5}\left(\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3 + \mathbf{v}_4 + \mathbf{v}_{\text{liked}}\right), \qquad
\mathbf{d}_- = \frac{1}{5}\left(\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3 + \mathbf{v}_4 + \mathbf{v}_{\text{disliked}}\right)
$$

The difference is

$$
\mathbf{d}_+ - \mathbf{d}_- = \frac{1}{5}\left(\mathbf{v}_{\text{liked}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{disliked}}\right),
$$

Be careful reading that $1/5$: it scales the shared words too, and cosine is
invariant to a common factor, so the factor itself is not the problem. What
matters is the *ratio* — one differing vector against four shared ones. Lengthen
the review to twenty words and there is still one differing vector, but now
nineteen shared ones instead of four, so the two documents' directions
converge. *The longer
the review, the more completely the shared content drowns out the word that
changed its meaning.*

Worse, in a subword model $\mathbf{v}_{\text{liked}}$ and
$\mathbf{v}_{\text{disliked}}$ are not even far apart, because `beğendim` and
`beğenmedim` share the n-grams `beğ`, `eğe`, `ğen`. fastText's own mechanism
pulls the difference $\mathbf{v}_{\text{liked}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{disliked}}$
towards zero.

TF-IDF has the opposite structure. `beğendim` and `beğenmedim` are two
distinct columns; a document containing one has a hard zero in the other, so
the contrast is explicit rather than averaged away. It is not immune to
dilution — with L2 normalisation, two $n$-term documents differing in one term
(each term used once, all weights equal, i.e. before IDF) sit at cosine
$(n-1)/n$, which also goes to 1 as $n$ grows. What differs is the
rate and the mechanism: the distinct columns keep the contrast on the page, and
IDF can weight it up. That is why its cosines land at 0.19 rather than 0.78 on
reviews of this length.

**The analogy.** Averaging word vectors is taking the mean colour of a
painting. Two paintings that differ only in that one is a sunrise and the
other a sunset have nearly the same mean colour, and the mean colour is the
only thing your classifier gets to see. A bag of words is instead a list of
which pigments appear — rougher about relationships, but it never loses the
one pigment that changed.
:::

Note what the classifier still manages in spite of this. Averaged fastText
assigns "ürünü çok beğendim" probability 0.82 of being positive and its
negation 0.02 — it gets the sign right even at cosine 0.776, because logistic
regression can find a direction in which the small remaining difference
between the two averages is discriminative. Watering the signal down is not
the same as deleting it. But it is a much harder problem handed to a linear
model, and it is a plausible part of the 14.8-point gap — a contributor, not
the whole explanation, since this chapter did not measure how much of the gap
it accounts for.

## The crossover: when embeddings do win

Everything so far has compared methods with 40,000 labelled reviews. That is
a luxury. The question that actually decides representation choice in
practice is: *how many labels do you have?*

The embedding models were trained without labels — they read the raw text and
learned from co-occurrence alone. That knowledge is already paid for before
the first review is annotated. TF-IDF's head start is far weaker: its axes
are just words, and everything it knows about sentiment must come out of the
labelled set. To be exact, TF-IDF does take something from the unlabelled
data — its IDF weights come from all 40,000 documents — but what it takes is
only document frequencies. It learns the vocabulary, not the meaning.

So hold the representations fixed and vary only the number of labels the
classifier sees.

```text
### macro-F1 by labelled training size (same test set of 10,000)
    n     negatives   tf-idf   tf-idf char   word2vec   fastText
   100        6        48.37       48.37       53.51      53.87
   250       16        48.53       48.84       61.59      63.10
   500       32        49.28       50.60       61.02      61.16
 1,000       63        55.40       58.55       59.52      59.93
 2,500      158        66.61       68.36       60.91      61.19
 5,000      316        71.16       70.47       61.52      60.80
10,000      632        72.55       71.29       61.80      61.56
20,000    1,264        72.42       71.26       60.94      60.96
40,000    2,529        71.95       70.39       61.39      61.36
```

Read the word2vec column downwards before reading anything else. From 250
labels to 40,000 — a 160-fold increase in training data — it goes 61.59, 61.02,
59.52, 60.91, 61.52, 61.80, 60.94, 61.39: an irregular swing of about 2.3
points that has no relationship to the amount of data. [Take that as a rough
indication of variability — not a noise floor in the technical sense — of how
much this design moves for reasons unrelated to the thing being
measured.]{.hl}

Be exact about what it is not. A noise floor is the spread of *repeated runs of
the same experiment*; these eight points differ in training size and in which
documents were sampled, so they mix real curve shape with run-to-run variation
and cannot be separated here. Still, a swing of 2.3 points with no trend across
a 160-fold change in data is hard to read as signal, and it is a single run with
a single seed. The honest consequence is that this chapter cannot *resolve*
differences of a point or two — `bag of words` against `tf-idf` (1.56), `tf-idf`
against `tf-idf char` (1.56), and word2vec against fastText (0.03) are all in
that range. Settling them takes what exercise 8 asks for: repeated runs at a
fixed training size, and a paired bootstrap over the test set.
