```{=html}
    <circle cx="554" cy="86.8" r="3"/><circle cx="627" cy="87.6" r="3"/><circle cx="700" cy="90.6" r="3"/>
  </g>

  <!-- labels -->
  <text x="90" y="118" class="t-sm t-rose t-b">averaged fastText</text>
  <text x="90" y="131" class="t-xs t-muted">knows the language before the first label</text>
  <text x="560" y="76" class="t-sm t-end t-accent t-b">tf-idf</text>
  <text x="704" y="114" class="t-xs t-end t-muted">learns everything from labels</text>

  <line x1="70" y1="312" x2="710" y2="312" class="ln-thin"/>
  <text x="70" y="326" class="t-xs t-muted">ON THIS DATA: UNDER ~1,500 LABELS → COORDINATES.  MORE → COUNTS.  SAME METHODS, DIFFERENT BUDGET.</text>
</svg>
```

::: {.fig-cap}
Three of the table's four representations (word TF-IDF, averaged fastText,
and averaged word2vec as the unlabelled dashed line; the character column is
left off for readability), nine training sizes, the same test set throughout;
the only variable is how much labelled data the classifier is given. At 250
labels averaged fastText is 14.6 macro-F1 points *ahead* of word TF-IDF
(word2vec 13.1); at 40,000 both embedding models are 10.6 points behind. Both of chapter 2's and chapter 3's claims are true — they are true
in different regimes, and the regime is set by your annotation budget.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Do not read that crossover as a transferable number.** The "≈ 1,500 labels"
on the chart is a result observed on this dataset, in this setup, on this
split: an exploratory demonstration, not a threshold to ship. Three reasons at
once. It uses a single seed and a single sequence of subsamples, so no
interval is attached to either curve; it should be repeated stratified
subsamples per `n`, reported as a mean with a 95% interval. The threshold was
read off the test set, which is also serving as the *selection* set — the
thing this chapter called indefensible up front; the right version splits
`train` again and reads the crossover on the inner slice. And the chapter's
actual winner is not on the chart: word bigram TF-IDF was never plotted. If it
sits above unigram TF-IDF at the left edge too, the crossover moves *left* —
but that was not measured, and with 3.4 times as many columns to estimate from
a handful of negatives it could just as well sit below.

What transfers is not the threshold but the shape: in a low-label regime a
representation learned from unlabelled text can have a head start, and as
labels accumulate the sparse linear model closes it. Plot your own curve for
your own task.
:::

Read the left edge of that chart carefully. **With 250 labelled reviews — of
which 16 are negative — TF-IDF scores 48.53, essentially the do-nothing
baseline's 48.37.** It fails to beat the baseline in macro-F1 — which is not the same
as having learned nothing; the same aggregate score does not mean the same
predictions, but there is no measurable gain on the decision metric. Averaged
fastText scores 63.10
with the same 250 labels, which is better than TF-IDF manages with 1,000.

The pattern is consistent with the following mechanism.

With 16 negative examples, TF-IDF sees 16 sparse rows drawn from a
30,195-dimensional space. A word appearing in one of them and nowhere else
can get a large coefficient supported by a single observation, and the model
generalises to nothing.

The embedding models started somewhere else entirely. They read all 903,190
tokens of unlabelled text before any label existed, so word2vec, for example,
already places `kalitesiz`, `dandik` and `dayanıksız` in the same region (the
neighbour lists above). Sixteen negative examples (and 234 positive ones)
are then enough to learn *which side of a boundary that region falls on* — one
decision in 100 dimensions instead of thirty thousand.

::: {.column-margin}
This is the general principle behind every pretrained model in this book,
visible in miniature. Self-supervised training converts unlabelled text into a
representation in which the supervised problem is low-dimensional. The
embeddings do not know about sentiment; they know about Turkish, and knowing
about Turkish is most of the work when you have sixteen examples.
:::

And then the curve flattens. Averaged fastText is at 61.16 with 500 labels
and 61.36 with 40,000 — **eighty times the supervision for two tenths of a
point.** The information bottleneck is no longer the labels, it is the
representation: once you have averaged a review into 100 numbers, the
distinction between "the shipping was fast" and "the shipping was slow" is
partly gone, and no quantity of labels restores it. TF-IDF, meanwhile, keeps
climbing until about 10,000 labels because each new label can sharpen an
individual word's coefficient.

**Two curves, two different limits: here the averaging-based static dense
setup is limited by its representation, and the sparse linear model is limited
by its labels.** Keeping the sentence that narrow matters — what was measured
is not "dense representations" but *this* setup: averaged 100-dimensional
static vectors trained from scratch. What generalises is asking which *kind*
of limit you are against: is my bottleneck labels, or representation?

## What it costs

We now know which method wins, and at what number of labels. Neither of those
is what a reviewer will ask you first.

The score is not the only axis. Now put cost next to performance — not "the
whole bill", only the three axes this experiment measured. The size of the
model artifact, the memory taken by the vocabulary and embedding table, the
size of the classifier itself, peak RAM during training, 95th-percentile (p95) latency and the
cost of deploying an index are all absent here.

```text
### cost, on one CPU core, 40,000 training documents (single run, not repeated)
                      build the        vectorise      training
                      representation   10,000 test    matrix
tf-idf                     0.5 s          0.11 s        9.7 MB
tf-idf 1-2 gram            0.9 s          0.17 s       15.4 MB
tf-idf char_wb 3-5         2.9 s          0.72 s      144.8 MB
word2vec + averaging      14.7 s          0.11 s       16.0 MB
fastText + averaging      31.6 s          0.27 s       16.0 MB
doc2vec                    8.5 s          1.73 s       16.0 MB
```

Two entries deserve comment.

**Character n-grams are expensive out of proportion to their benefit.** 144.8
MB and 301 non-zeros per document, for 70.39 macro-F1 — worse than plain
word tf-idf at 9.7 MB — fifteen times the memory for a lower macro-F1. (The
bag-of-words matrix has the same sparsity pattern and therefore the same size;
only the tf-idf row appears in the table.) They are the right tool when spelling is the problem
(and at 1,000 labels, where they beat word TF-IDF by 3.2 points, they were
the better of the two sparse methods on the learning curve), but they are not a free upgrade.

**doc2vec must run gradient descent to vectorise a new document.** 1.73
seconds for 10,000 reviews, against 0.11 for averaging — a 16-fold difference,
and unlike training that cost recurs on every new document. Look at the
absolute number too: 0.17 milliseconds per document is still small for most
services, and the decision belongs to your latency budget. Combined with the
worst macro-F1 in the comparison (55.13), the recommendation this chapter can
support is: **do not make doc2vec your default on a short, noisy
classification task like this one** — there is no performance-cost case for
it.
@sec-embeddings had it ahead of averaging on 20 Newsgroups; on 40,000 short,
noisy Turkish reviews it is 6.3 points behind. Long, clean documents are the
regime where learning a document vector pays, and reviews are neither.

### The hybrid, and an honest negative result

One caveat first, because it narrows what the negative result below covers.
The two blocks arrive on different scales: `char_wb` TF-IDF rows are
L2-normalised, so their ~301 non-zeros are each around 0.06, while the averaged
fastText components run an order of magnitude larger across 100 columns.
Handing that to a single L2-penalised `C = 1.0` means the relative weight of
the two blocks was chosen by the default rather than by us. Normalising each
block separately and searching a mixing coefficient is the version worth
refuting; what follows refutes the cheap concatenation, which is a narrower
claim.

The obvious move is to concatenate: character TF-IDF for spelling robustness,
averaged fastText for semantics, one classifier over both.

```text
### tf-idf char_wb 3-5  ⊕  averaged fastText   (95,039 dimensions)
accuracy   89.36     macro-F1   71.65     F1(neg)   49.24
```

It beats both of its parts — char TF-IDF alone scored 70.39, fastText alone
61.36 — and it still loses to plain word bigrams by 4.6 points.

It also costs far more to build: **34.5 seconds** against the bigram model's
**0.9**, because the hybrid has to fit the character vectoriser (2.9 s) *and*
train fastText (31.6 s), both from the cost table above.

So concatenation is a real technique and this is a real gain over the
components. It did not rescue the dense representation — and reporting it as a
success by comparing only against its own parts would be exactly the kind of
selective baseline this chapter is arguing against.

## Choosing, on purpose

Seven methods, one dataset, and enough measurements to stop guessing. Here is
the whole thing as a decision rather than a leaderboard.

| | [Strengths]{.pro} | [Weaknesses]{.con} | Choose it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bag of words** | Fastest to build and reason about. Beat TF-IDF here at a fixed `C = 1.0`. Coefficients readable word by word. | No length normalisation; long documents dominate. Applies no global informativeness weighting at the representation stage; it leaves that to the downstream classifier. | You want a baseline in five minutes that is genuinely hard to beat, and your documents are short. |
| **TF-IDF (words)** | The standard strong baseline. Down-weights ubiquitous words. Trivially interpretable and auditable. | [Lost]{.con} to raw counts on this short-review corpus under a shared, untuned `C` — and edged ahead of them (by 1.2 points, inside this chapter's noise) once both got an equal tuning budget, so measure both on short text. One column per word form: up to 895 forms for one Turkish verb family. Zero generalisation to unseen forms. | A general-purpose first sparse baseline — just remember to tune `C` on a validation set. |
| **TF-IDF (word bigrams)** | Best score in this chapter, 76.21. Captures multi-word negation that unigrams miss. Still a linear model you can read. | 3.4× the columns. Still blind to unseen vocabulary. | You have labels and the task turns on short phrases — sentiment, intent, triage. A strong first sparse baseline to build for short-text classification. |
| **TF-IDF (char n-grams)** | Robust to spelling: a misspelt word still shares most of its n-grams with the correct one. (The vectoriser does learn a finite n-gram vocabulary and discards unseen n-grams — the point is that a new *word* rarely produces only new n-grams.) Strongest sparse method on the learning curve's low-label end (bigrams were not tested there). Less dependent on a word tokeniser — but lowercasing, Unicode normalisation and broken characters are still language-specific decisions. | 144.8 MB and 301 non-zeros per document. Lower macro-F1 than plain counting at full data. Coefficients are not human-readable. | Spelling is unreliable, the language is agglutinative, or you have no trustworthy tokeniser. |
| **Averaged word2vec** | 100 dimensions for 61.4 macro-F1 — 302× fewer dimensions than word tf-idf. Trained without labels. On this dataset, [ahead of both sparse methods tested here]{.pro} below roughly 1,500 labels — the threshold itself does not transfer. Semantic neighbours you can inspect. | `KeyError` on 46.4% of the distinct word forms in the test set. Confident nonsense on rare in-vocabulary words. Averaging dilutes negation. Word order gone. | Labels are scarce, or you need compact vectors for similarity search over millions of documents. |
| **Averaged fastText** | Every string gets a vector — coverage is 100% by construction. Handles the missing diacritics and typos in real user text. Best of the methods on the learning curve at 250 labels. | Neighbours are [orthographic, not semantic]{.con}: `kalitesiz` → `kalitesi`. 2× word2vec's training time. Bought perfect coverage for no macro-F1 gain here (−0.03). | The text is user-generated and misspelled, the language is agglutinative, and you cannot control the input vocabulary. |
| **doc2vec** | One vector per document with no averaging heuristic. Learns document-level structure averaging cannot. | [Worst]{.con} score here, 55.13. Inference needs gradient steps: 16× slower per document, forever. Extra hyperparameters. | It may be worth trying where documents are long and clean — that is a hypothesis this chapter did not measure — and only once you have measured that it beats averaging on *your* data. |

: What to reach for, and why {tbl-colwidths="[13,30,30,27]"}

The decision procedure, compressed to something you can apply before writing
any code. Note what it is: a list of questions, not a list of thresholds.

```text
### how to choose, in order
1. Write down the task and the decision metric.
2. Measure two budgets: how many labels you have, how much unlabelled text.
3. Build at least three cheap baselines:
     word counts / tf-idf
     word n-grams
     character n-grams   (especially if the spelling is noisy)
4. If you have a strong unlabelled corpus, add a pretrained or
   domain-trained embedding baseline.
5. Audit the vocabulary: OOV rate, spelling, morphology.
6. Read the error pairs. Do the errors come from order/negation,
   or from spelling/OOV?
7. For each candidate, write down four numbers together:
     score + interval   ·   latency   ·   memory   ·   explainability need
8. Make the decision on a validation set.
9. Open the test set once.
```

The numbers this chapter observed — the crossover around 1,500 labels, the
counts-versus-tf-idf ordering on short documents — are useful as *expectations*
at step 4, not as rules at step 1. The same goes for "sparse if you need an
explanation" and "dense if you need similarity search over millions of
vectors": both are strong first candidates, not absolutes. Sparse lexical
retrieval can be entirely standard over millions of documents, and dense
models can be made explainable.

## The failure they share

It would be a poor summary to leave you with "counting won".

Because here is a question the whole chapter has avoided. Both families were
scored on the same test set, and the winner was 15 points ahead — so what does
the *winner* still get wrong, and is it the same thing the loser gets wrong?

It is. Both families fail in the same place, and that shared failure is the
reason there is a Part II.

```text
### two reviews, same words, opposite meaning
a = "kalite iyi fiyat kötü"      (quality good, price bad)
b = "kalite kötü fiyat iyi"      (quality bad, price good)

cosine, averaged fastText   1.0000
cosine, tf-idf              1.0000
```

Not approximately equal. **Identical** — exactly so in exact arithmetic, and
up to floating-point rounding (far below the fourth decimal) in practice.
TF-IDF sees the same four words with the same counts. Averaging sees the same
four vectors summed in a different order, and addition is commutative. Neither representation contains the information that
would distinguish a complaint about price from a complaint about quality,
so no classifier built on top of them can ever recover it — not with more
labels, not with a better classifier, not ever.

Document-level sentiment can tolerate this loss better than aspect-level
tasks; that most reviews are entirely positive or entirely negative is a
reasonable expectation, but this chapter did not measure it. For "which
component is the customer complaining about", the same loss directly blocks
the task.

Label that 1.0000 precisely, because one family in this chapter escapes it.
The two rows above are **unigram TF-IDF and averaged embeddings**. Word
bigrams are a different matter: `kalite iyi`, `iyi fiyat`, `fiyat kötü` against
`kalite kötü`, `kötü fiyat`, `fiyat iyi` share no bigram at all, so this
chapter's *winning* model — word 1–2 grams — separates this pair cleanly when
those features survive `min_df`. Widening the unit does buy local order.

What it does not buy is order in general. A bag of bigrams is still a bag: it
sees a fixed window and nothing beyond it. In *the pump the engineer replaced
last week failed*, five words separate `pump` from `failed`; only a 7-gram
spans that link, and a 7-gram is so specific that it will almost never occur
twice. Whatever window you fix, some dependency is longer, and the vocabulary
cost of chasing it grows exponentially with the window size. To handle that the representation has to be a
function of the *sequence*: something that reads `kalite`, then `iyi`, and produces a
different state than if it had read `kalite`, then `kötü`. That takes us to
sequence-aware encoders. Language models are one important way of learning
such encoders from large amounts of unlabelled text, and @sec-language-models
starts there — but a sequence-aware encoder does not have to be a language
model. The mechanism that makes that state depend on every other word at once
is attention, and it is @sec-transformers.

The bake-off has told us exactly what to demand of them: keep TF-IDF's
sensitivity to the individual decisive word, keep embeddings' generalisation
across word forms and their tiny label appetite, and add the one thing
neither has — order.

## Intuition checks

Answer before expanding.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your client has 400 labelled support tickets in Turkish and 2 million unlabelled ones. Which representation?

Averaged fastText, and the second sentence of the question is why.

At 400 labels you are on the left of the crossover chart, where TF-IDF is
still near the do-nothing baseline — at 500 labels it scored 49.28 against
fastText's 61.16. Two million unlabelled tickets is a large free corpus for
self-supervised training. Do not read that as "a count model cannot use
unlabelled data" — this chapter's own TF-IDF learned its vocabulary and IDF
weights from all 40,000 documents without looking at a label. The difference
is *what can be learned*: TF-IDF is limited to vocabulary and document
frequency, while an embedding model can extract co-occurrence structure and
subword geometry from the same text — far richer unsupervised information.

Choose fastText over word2vec because the tickets are Turkish and
user-written: 46.4% of the test set's distinct word forms were outside the
trained vocabulary here; support tickets may well be noisier still, but audit
that on your own data rather than assuming it.

Then say the second half out loud: *label 2,000 more tickets and re-run this
comparison*. This chapter's bake-off suggests the sparse side can take the
advantage within a few thousand labels — but that threshold belongs to this
dataset; plot your own learning curve.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. A colleague reports 93% accuracy and wants to ship. What do you ask for?

The confusion matrix, and then the macro-F1.

93% is below the 93.68% you get by predicting the majority class for every
input, so on this dataset that model may be worse than a constant. The two
follow-up questions: how many of the 632 negatives did it find, and what
happens downstream to the ones it missed?

The general form of the question is *what is the accuracy of the trivial
baseline* — and you should ask it before you look at any reported score, not
after.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. fastText fixed the out-of-vocabulary problem completely. Why did the score not move?

Because coverage was apparently not what limited the score.

Coverage went from 53.6% of word forms to 100%, and macro-F1 went from 61.39 to
61.36. Read the comparison for what it is: two models trained by different
methods, so it does not isolate coverage — fastText's subword vectors differ
from word2vec's in more ways than one. What it does show is that buying perfect
coverage did not pay here, and the chapter's other measurements point at
averaging as the reason: averaged fastText places a sentence and its negation
at cosine 0.78–0.96. (Only fastText went through that probe; the averaging
argument applies to word2vec equally, but its cosines were not measured.)

There is also a cost hiding in the fix. fastText spends its capacity on
character n-grams, so its nearest neighbours become morphological rather than
semantic — `kalitesiz` ("low quality") retrieves `kalitesi` ("its quality"),
a neutral form that has lost the negative polarity.
One possible explanation: it gained coverage and lost some meaning, and the two roughly cancelled. We did not measure that; separating the two effects takes its own experiment.

The transferable lesson: an intrinsic improvement only shows up extrinsically
if the thing it improved was the bottleneck. Measure which one you have
before you fix either.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Would 300-dimensional vectors, or pretrained ones, have changed the verdict?

They would move the numbers and not the shape. That first clause is an
expectation, not a measurement — neither variant was run here, and the
reasoning below is why you would expect it, not evidence that it holds.

Larger vectors and pretrained Turkish embeddings
[@grave2018learning] would
be expected to lift the dense curve — probably a few points, and more at the
left edge where extra pretraining data matters most. What they cannot do is fix
averaging — but separate the two results, because only one of them is a
property of the mean. The exactly-1.0000 word-order figure is: averaging is
invariant to permutation, so no vectors change it. The 0.78–0.96 negation
cosines are not; those sentences differ in *which* word appears, and better
vectors could put `beğendim` and `beğenmedim` further apart. Pretraining might
move those numbers and might move the crossover with them. This chapter did not
measure by how much, and neither claim above should be read as settled.

The way to settle it is exercise 13: rerun this chapter's script with
300-dimensional pretrained vectors and report whether the crossover moves past your actual label budget.
That is the only version of the question that affects a decision.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-bake-off-interview}

Representation choice is the most common design question in an applied NLP
screen, and the most common wrong answer is to name the newest method. Almost
every answer below rests on something this chapter measured, so you can quote a
number instead of a preference.

::: {.column-margin}
The pattern in all six: name the axis the question is really about — labels,
morphology, structure, cost — then give the measurement, then say what would
change your answer. An answer with no number is an opinion; an answer with no
*condition* is a slogan.
:::

1. **Embeddings or TF-IDF for text classification?** Ask how many labels they
   have; that is the first axis, not the only one — the size of the unlabelled
   corpus, the structure of the task (document-level or aspect-level),
   document length and spelling/OOV noise all move the answer too. On this corpus the
   curves cross at roughly **1,500 labels**: at 250 labels averaged fastText
   scores 63.10 macro-F1 against word TF-IDF's 48.53 — essentially the
   do-nothing baseline — and at 40,000 that same TF-IDF scores 71.95 against 61.36. Note
   which model that is. Bigram TF-IDF, this chapter's actual winner, reaches
   76.21 at 40,000 but is not on the learning curve at all; if it also sits
   above word TF-IDF on the left of the curve, the crossover moves *left* —
   that was not measured. The threshold you read off a curve depends on which
   sparse model you put on it. The embeddings
   were trained without labels, so their knowledge is paid for before the first
   annotation; TF-IDF has to buy everything it knows out of the labelled set.
   Finish with the shape, and with its limit: [this from-scratch averaged
   embedding curve plateaus by 500 labels; the sparse one climbs until roughly 10,000 and then flattens]{.hl} —
   72.55 at 10,000 against 71.95 at 40,000, a difference well inside this
   experiment's noise. So the more labels you expect *up to about ten
   thousand*, the more the answer tilts sparse; past that, neither curve is
   buying you much and the next move is a different model family rather than
   more annotation.

2. **Why would averaging word vectors lose to counting words?** Because
   averaging destroys the thing sentiment lives in. Measured directly: a review
   and its negation sit at cosine **0.78 to 0.96** under averaged fastText and
   **0.19 to 0.69** under TF-IDF. The mean of a handful of vectors is dominated
   by the words the two sentences *share*, and in a negated pair that is nearly
   all of them — the one word carrying the reversal is averaged into nothing.
   The good version of this answer names the fix as well: weighted averaging
   with the first principal component removed [@arora2017simple] is the
   cheapest thing to try before reaching for an encoder.

3. **Turkish is morphologically rich. Which method does that argue for?**
   fastText over word2vec, and the number to quote is not the token rate. On
   this test set 7.27% of *tokens* were outside the word2vec vocabulary, which
   sounds survivable — but **46.4% of the distinct word forms** were outside it, so nearly
   half the distinct forms in that test set are a `KeyError` — and the rate
   varies by batch and domain. fastText covers 100% by
   construction because it sums character n-grams. Then deliver the twist,
   because it is the part that shows you measured rather than assumed:
   [fixing out-of-vocabulary coverage completely moved macro-F1 by 0.03
   points]{.hl}, 61.39 to 61.36. Coverage was not the bottleneck here; the
   chapter's other probes point at averaging instead.

4. **How would you compare two representations beyond their headline
   scores?** Stop looking at the aggregate and cross-tabulate the paired
   predictions. Plain word TF-IDF and averaged fastText agree on 84.1% of the
   test set; where they disagree TF-IDF is right 1,315 times and averaged
   fastText 272 — nearly five to one, and those two counts are also what a
   McNemar test needs. Then read the 272: the examples this chapter looked at
   are missing diacritics and colloquial spellings, exactly what a subword
   model should win (a systematic count of all 272 was not done). That
   suggests the two are partly complementary, which is a different decision
   from "one is better" — and the same procedure matters most when two models
   score within a point of each other, where the aggregate cannot separate
   them.

5. **What does the cheap method cost, and does that matter?** Have the numbers.
   TF-IDF 1-2 gram: 0.9 s to build, 0.17 s to vectorise 10,000 documents,
   15.4 MB. fastText: 31.6 s to train, 16.0 MB. Both are trivial, which is the
   point — [at this scale the cost axis does not decide anything, so do not
   pretend it does]{.hl}. Say that plainly. Cost becomes the deciding axis at
   the scale of @sec-classification-crossover, where a prompted model costs 142×
   more per document than a fine-tuned encoder, and knowing *when* an axis
   starts mattering is the skill being tested.

6. **Everything here is beaten by a fine-tuned encoder. Why learn it?** Two
   reasons, and the second is the real one. First, the crossover is real:
   below roughly 500 labels the encoder in @sec-classification-finetune is
   worse than both methods in this chapter. Second, this chapter is where the
   *diagnostic* habits come from — the negation-cosine probe, the
   disagreement cross-tabulation, the coverage-versus-score distinction. Those
   transfer to every model you will ever ship. A candidate who can only run
   `AutoModel.from_pretrained` cannot tell you why their model fails.

| [Hugging Face LLM Course](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course) | formerly the NLP Course; free and runnable; it starts from the transformer models this book reaches in Part II, so read it as the next step after this chapter's classical baselines |

: Beyond the papers {tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}

Note that the name "fastText" covers two different things: **unsupervised
subword word vectors** (what round 2 of this chapter used) and the
**supervised fastText classifier** (the first paper below). They come from the
same library but they are not the same thing.

- **fastText for classification** [@joulin2017bag]. A linear model over
  averaged word and word-n-gram embeddings, trained in minutes on a CPU,
  reported as "on par with deep learning classifiers". A close relative of this
  chapter's round 2 (average the vectors, then a linear classifier), and still an excellent production answer for
  high-volume, low-latency routing.
- **Enriching word vectors with subword information**
  [@bojanowski2017enriching]. The paper behind the coverage result above;
  its experiments centre on morphologically rich languages (Czech, German and
  Russian among them), the setting where subwords help most.
- **Distributed representations of sentences and documents**
  [@le2014distributed]. doc2vec's original claims, worth reading against this
  chapter's measurement of it.
- **A simple but tough-to-beat baseline for sentence embeddings**
  [@arora2017simple]. Weighted averaging with the first principal component
  removed — the cheapest realistic upgrade to round 2, and the first thing to
  try if you want to move the dense curve.
- **The Hitchhiker's Guide to Testing Statistical Significance in NLP**
  [@dror2018hitchhikers]. The protocol exercise 8 asks for, and exactly what
  is missing to settle this chapter's adjacent differences.
- **scikit-learn** [@pedregosa2011scikit] and **gensim**
  [@rehurek2010software]. The two libraries this chapter is built from; the
  user guides are unusually good.

## Exercises

The label on each exercise marks its level: **Basic** consolidates a concept,
**Applied** makes you measure something on your own data, **Advanced** goes
past this chapter, and **Research** is open-ended.

1. **Move the crossover.** *(Applied)* Rerun the learning curve with `min_df=1` and with
   `min_df=5` for TF-IDF. Predict first which direction the low-label end
   moves, then check. Explain the result in terms of how many observations
   support each coefficient.
2. **Kill the imbalance instead.** *(Basic)* Drop `class_weight="balanced"` and rerun
   every model. Report accuracy *and* macro-F1 for each. Which methods
   collapse to the majority class? Does the ranking by accuracy change more
   than the ranking by macro-F1 — and if so, why?
3. **Weighted averaging.** *(Advanced)* Implement @arora2017simple: average the word
   vectors with weight $a/(a + p(w))$ for $a = 10^{-3}$, then remove the
   first principal component of the resulting document matrix. Report the
   new dense scores. Did it beat plain averaging, and did it close any of
   the 14.8-point gap?
4. **The negation probe, extended.** *(Applied)* Build twenty negation pairs from your
   own domain and measure both cosines. Then find the pair with the highest
   averaged-embedding cosine that the classifier *still* gets right, and
   explain how it can.
5. **Break the char n-gram model.** *(Applied)* Character n-grams were the better of the two
   sparse methods on the learning curve at 1,000 labels, and the worst sparse
   method at 40,000. Construct the
   argument for why, using the number of features and the number of
   observations per feature, then test it by varying `min_df`.
6. **A different task, same pipeline.** *(Research)* Swap sentiment for a task where the
   bag is insufficient — for example, labelling which aspect (shipping,
   price, quality) a review complains about. Predict what happens to the gap
   between counting and embeddings before you run it, then run it.
7. **Repair the case-conversion damage.** *(Applied)* Running round 1 with `str.lower()` on
   *this* corpus changes nothing, for the reason given above — there is no
   uppercase left to get wrong. The damage was done upstream instead: 4,194
   documents carry a stray U+0307. Strip it, re-tokenise, and rerun the round-1
   table. Report the change in vocabulary size and in macro-F1, then say which
   of the two you expected to move more, and why.
8. **Supply the intervals this chapter does not have.** *(Advanced — not a
   bonus but basic experimental science for this chapter's subject; if you do
   only one of these, do this one.)* Bootstrap the 10,000
   test rows 1,000 times and put a 95% interval on every row of the combined
   leaderboard. Then run a paired test on each adjacent pair — McNemar for the
   accuracy column, a paired bootstrap for macro-F1, since McNemar tests error
   rates and not F1. Report which of the seven gaps
   survive and which do not, and rewrite the ranking sentence accordingly. Then
   repeat the whole chapter with five seeds and see how much of your answer was
   the seed. @dror2018hitchhikers is the protocol.

9. **Ship one.** *(Applied)* Take the winning configuration, write the confusion matrix
   at three different decision thresholds, and choose one — writing the
   sentence that justifies the choice to whoever handles the false alarms.
   That sentence, not the macro-F1, is the actual deliverable.
10. **Is IDF really the culprit?** *(Applied)* Rerun the ablation ladder from
    this chapter yourself — raw counts, counts + L2, log-TF + L2, TF-IDF —
    then add one rung: repeat every row with `C` tuned on a validation set.
    How much of the normalisation effect survives?
11. **Analyzer audit.** *(Basic)* Write ten sentences containing punctuation,
    digits, an emoji and a U+0307. Put the features produced by
    `analyzer="word"` next to those produced by `char_wb`. Write down what
    extra material the character arm sees, and how that affects the round 1
    comparison.
12. **Repeated learning curves.** *(Research)* For each `n` on the learning
    curve, draw 20 stratified subsamples and report the mean and a 95%
    interval for each representation. Report the crossover as a distribution
    rather than a single number — and put bigram TF-IDF on the curve too.
13. **Rerun with pretrained vectors.** *(Advanced)* Replace round 2's
    from-scratch vectors with the 300-dimensional pretrained Turkish fastText
    vectors [@grave2018learning] and redraw
    the learning curve on the same test set. First predict at which end the
    dense curve will rise more and which way the crossover will move. Then
    measure it, and report whether the crossover moves past your actual label
    budget. Did the cosine of the `kalite iyi fiyat kötü` pair change?
